overview: In the first week after the midterm elections, President Trump said on "60 Minutes" that his deportation policy "might be too tough", while Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff and Democrats prepare oversight investigations. On Wall Street, a sharp selloff in AI and data-center stocks on Nov. 5 left markets unsettled, and a strong October jobs report kept a possible December Fed rate hike in play. In New York, a former police officer and school aide was charged with murder in the stabbing of a jogger in Brooklyn, and Mayor Mamdani announced $25 million for cold-weather outreach.

stories.headline: Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' after midterm losses
stories.summary: In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday, President Trump said his deportation policy "might be too tough" in the wake of Republican losses in last week's midterm elections. The Guardian reported he also offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats. The remarks came as Stephen Miller, the architect of the crackdown, started as chief of staff.
stories.why_it_matters: Any softening of deportation enforcement or a bipartisan immigration deal would change risks for immigrant families and employers. Whether the comments lead to policy change is not yet clear.
stories.background: Mass deportation has been a defining policy of Trump's second term, run by the Department of Homeland Security and ICE. Democrats won a large House majority and gains elsewhere in the Nov. 3 midterms, and outlets point to immigration enforcement and the economy as factors in voters' choices. Trump has not announced any change to enforcement operations. Miller, who shaped the policy, took over as White House chief of staff on Monday.

facts.text: Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview aired Sunday that his deportation policy "might be too tough," according to The New York Times.
France 24 reported the interview came days after Republicans suffered heavy midterm losses.
Deutsche Welle reported Trump said the policy may be one of the reasons Republicans lost ground.

stories.headline: Stephen Miller starts as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
stories.summary: Stephen Miller, Trump's deputy chief of staff and a leading voice on immigration, is due to begin as chief of staff on Monday. Trump announced the change on Nov. 6, days after the midterms. Deputy chief of staff Richard Walters is leaving ahead of the handover, Fox News reported.
stories.why_it_matters: The chief of staff controls access to the president and shapes which policies advance, so the choice signals the direction of the administration's remaining term. Miller's record points to continued emphasis on immigration enforcement.
stories.background: Miller has been among Trump's closest aides for years and was a principal designer of the immigration crackdown. Susie Wiles, the previous chief of staff, is moving to Trump's political operation, per reports. The change followed Democratic gains in the midterm elections held on Nov. 3. The chief of staff post does not require Senate confirmation.

facts.text: Miller is replacing Susie Wiles as chief of staff; The Hindu described her as the first major White House departure after the Democratic midterm win.

stories.headline: Trump and Justice Department push back as Democrats prepare investigations
stories.summary: AP reported that Trump and the Justice Department are taking a combative stance toward Democrats' oversight plans after the midterms. Trump wrote that investigative requests already made are "extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable." Sen. Bernie Sanders separately urged Democrats not to spend all their time investigating the administration.
stories.why_it_matters: How aggressively the new House majority uses subpoenas and hearings will shape what the public learns about the administration and what gets done on costs such as health care and groceries. Fights over compliance could end up in court.
stories.background: Democrats won control of the House in the Nov. 3 midterms and are set to take committee gavels in January. Party leaders have signaled they will use oversight powers against the administration. Sanders said Democrats should stand up for working-class families, while also saying he is open to impeaching Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., per CNN's headline.

stories.headline: Jeffries says he is a 'hard yes' on impeaching Hegseth
stories.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" that he supports Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The Pentagon said Hegseth would not be deterred by "phony investigations," per the BBC. The New York Times said a reckoning could come before the new Congress begins.
stories.why_it_matters: A bipartisan impeachment push against the Pentagon chief would put pressure on the administration's war and defense policy. A vote in the lame-duck session would show whether any Republicans join.
stories.background: Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September, accusing him of abusing his powers in leading the US war with Iran, per Scripps News. Jeffries is expected to become House speaker when Democrats take the majority. Congress returns this week for its lame-duck session.

facts.text: Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" that he is a "hard yes" on impeaching Hegseth and supports Massie's effort.

stories.headline: Nvidia board investigates CEO Jensen Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative
stories.summary: Nvidia said its board launched an independent investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." The New York Times reported Huang acknowledged Sunday being intimate with a business executive U.S. officials determined worked for Chinese intelligence. Nvidia shares fell about 5%, per CNBC.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is a central company in AI chips and U.S.-China technology rivalry, so questions about its leader affect markets and export policy. Investors and retirement funds holding the stock feel moves in its price.
stories.background: A New York Times report published Oct. 29 said U.S. intelligence concluded that Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, passed information to Beijing, per web reports. Nvidia said earlier allegations about Megaspeed had been investigated, and Jensen Huang called the claims speculation. Sen. Elizabeth Warren asked Nvidia's board for answers. This past weekend, Huang apologized for an affair, per the Wall Street Journal's summary.

facts.text: Nvidia said its board launched an independent investigation, and the stock fell about 5%, per CNBC.
Huang acknowledged on Sunday being intimate with an executive U.S. officials determined was working for Chinese intelligence, per the NYT.

Bloomberg's headline put the loss in Nvidia's market value at about $200 billion.

stories.headline: After midterms, Trump and Democrats face pressure to deliver economic relief
stories.summary: An AP analysis says voters sent Trump and the new Democratic congressional majority a message to repair an economy hurt by inflation. PBS NewsHour's version says Trump, who maintained the economy is booming, has said since the election he is willing to work with Democrats.
stories.why_it_matters: Prices and affordability drive household budgets, and a divided government could either produce compromise or gridlock on them. Lame-duck decisions come first.
stories.background: Democrats won the House and made gains elsewhere in the Nov. 3 midterms. Trump had warned during the campaign that a Democratic win would bring a 1929-style economic depression, per PBS. Congress returns this week.

facts.text: Trump has maintained the economy is booming and, since his party's loss, has said he is willing to work with Democrats, per PBS NewsHour's version of the AP story.

stories.headline: Staff at federal AI safety center asked to report to the White House
stories.summary: AP sources say officials at the Commerce Department's AI center, known as CAISSI, were recently asked to informally report to a White House office, raising questions about independence. ABC reported the small division has no permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research.
stories.why_it_matters: The center is meant to assess the safety of new AI products, so its independence affects how much the public can rely on government evaluations of them.

stories.headline: Israel's president gives opposition leader Eisenkot first chance to form a government
stories.summary: President Isaac Herzog formally tasked opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot on Sunday evening with forming Israel's next government. Eisenkot now has about six weeks to assemble a coalition that could replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Coverage describes the coalition arithmetic as difficult.
stories.why_it_matters: Who governs Israel shapes the war and ceasefire diplomacy in Gaza and the region, and the coalition talks decide whether Netanyahu stays in office.
stories.background: Israel's parliament, the Knesset, is split between Netanyahu's bloc and a divided opposition. Under Israeli law the president picks the lawmaker most likely to command a majority and gives that person a set period to build a coalition. Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff who now leads an opposition party. Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister. If Eisenkot fails, the mandate can pass to another lawmaker.

facts.text: Herzog formally gave Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government on Sunday evening, Nov. 8.
Bloomberg reported Eisenkot had the endorsement of 67 members of the Knesset when he was tasked.

Bloomberg said he must build a coalition from a divided opposition while drawing allies away from Netanyahu.

stories.headline: Gunman who killed six in Krakow's Main Square dies in hospital
stories.summary: A 24-year-old gunman opened fire in Krakow's Old Town Main Square on Saturday, killing six people and wounding at least 15, police said. He was shot by police and died in hospital Monday. Poland declared two days of national mourning and officials are treating the attack as terrorism.
stories.why_it_matters: Mass shootings are rare in Poland, and the attack comes as political tension over far-right extremism rises ahead of a large nationalist march this week.
stories.background: Krakow's Main Square is one of Poland's best-known tourist sites. Poland has strict gun laws and has had few mass shootings. AP and others report the suspect had far-right views, and France 24 says the attack comes ahead of a major nationalist march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has called on politicians not to exploit the incident.

facts.text: Police said the 24-year-old gunman, wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into the Main Square and opened fire.
Six people were killed and 15 wounded, and the gunman died in hospital on Monday after being shot by police, according to AP.
AP reported the gunman had far-right views.
Poland began two days of national mourning.
Tusk called on politicians not to exploit the incident, the Financial Times reported.
CBS reported senior officials described the attack as an 'act of terror'.

positions.claim: Six killed and 15 wounded in the square, per AP and ABC.
Six killed, including a British man, and 16 injured, per The Guardian.
At least nine dead after shootings in Krakow and another town, per The New York Times; the BBC separately reported three bodies of the suspect's family members found at their home.

stories.headline: Houthi missile attack damages Aramco building in Riyadh as Saudi Arabia turns to Syria
stories.summary: Saudi Arabia said it intercepted Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh on Sunday, and falling debris damaged an Aramco office building in the capital's financial district. Saudi authorities said no one was hurt. Separately, AP reported Syria is preparing to send fighters to support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.
stories.why_it_matters: Strikes on Riyadh's business district and airport raise risks for oil infrastructure, flights and energy prices, and Syrian involvement could widen the conflict.
stories.background: The Houthis are an Iran-backed group that controls much of Yemen's north and has been fighting Saudi-backed forces. Bloomberg says a deadly strike on Riyadh's airport about a month ago disrupted travel and cancelled events. Aramco is Saudi Arabia's state oil company. Syria and Saudi Arabia have recently moved closer.

stories.headline: South Africa's ANC records worst-ever result in local elections
stories.summary: The African National Congress won about 30 percent of the vote in South Africa's Nov. 4 local elections with 99 percent of ballots counted, its worst showing. President Cyril Ramaphosa said the verdict must be respected, and coalition talks are expected.
stories.why_it_matters: Weak results for the governing party mean local councils responsible for water, electricity and services may be run by shaky coalitions.
stories.background: The ANC has led South Africa since the end of apartheid in 1994, and was the party of Nelson Mandela. It lost its national majority in 2024 and now governs in a coalition. DW reports voters blamed it for water and electricity shortages. No party won an outright majority in many places, so councils will need coalition deals.

facts.text: The ANC received around 30% of the vote with 99% of ballots counted, The Hindu reported.
Ramaphosa said the verdict must be respected, while the ANC's secretary-general called the outcome 'catastrophic', the BBC reported.

Reuters said the result sets up tough coalition talks.

stories.headline: Two passenger trains collide south of Cairo, killing at least seven

stories.background: The crash took place about 32 miles (52 km) south of Cairo. ABC and the NYT note Egypt has a history of deadly rail accidents, with the NYT adding this is despite billions spent on modernization. ABC says the system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance.

stories.headline: Pope Leo tells Argentina's Milei the economy must serve people
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Argentina, the second stop of a 12-day South American tour, and in remarks with President Javier Milei said people should come before the economy. Outlets differ on whether this was a direct or veiled criticism of Milei's austerity policies.
stories.why_it_matters: The visit puts the Church's social teaching in public tension with Argentina's budget cuts, which affect pensions and disability support.
stories.background: Leo, 71, is the first US-born pope and is touring three South American countries weeks after lung cancer surgery, CBS reported. Argentina is the home country of his predecessor Francis, who never returned during his 12-year papacy. stories.summary: Former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has asked Bangladesh's government for a new passport and identity card so she can return from exile in India, according to a letter seen by Reuters. stories.background: Hasina fled to India in August 2024 after a mass uprising toppled her government, and her passport was cancelled soon after. She has since been convicted in Bangladesh, and the country's Law Minister says an extradition request has been sent to India. Japan Times reports her plan is to return in December.

stories.headline: AI stocks stay shaky after the worst day for the S&P 500 since April 2025
stories.summary: A selloff in AI and data-center stocks on Thursday Nov. 5 pushed the S&P 500 down about 4.4%, and the market has been unsettled since. US futures rose Monday after a rough week, though Nvidia still unsettled investors, per Reuters. Citi strategists cut US stocks and global tech, and hedge funds sold tech at one of the fastest paces on record, per Bloomberg.
stories.why_it_matters: Big tech stocks make up a large share of the S&P 500, so swings in them move many people's 401(k)s and index funds. A lasting AI pullback could also affect investment in data centers and the jobs tied to them.
stories.background: Stocks tied to the AI buildout have driven much of the market's gains in recent years. After the Nov. 3 midterm elections, investors began to worry that Democratic gains could bring pauses or moratoriums on data-center construction. That fear, plus concern about financing, set off Thursday's drop, which AP reported as the S&P 500's worst day since the April 2025 tariff selloff. Asian markets, which also fell, mostly rebounded Monday, with South Korean and Taiwanese authorities having stepped in to limit losses, per the Wall Street Journal. China's state-led funds put a record amount into ETFs last week, per Bloomberg.

facts.text: AP reported the S&P 500 fell about 4.4% on Thursday, Nov. 5, its worst day since April 2025, in a selloff led by AI and data-center stocks.
AP and other reports tied the drop to fears that Democratic election gains could lead to moratoriums on data-center construction.
Reuters reported Wall Street futures rose Monday after a rough week, but that Nvidia unsettled investors.

Bloomberg reported hedge funds sold global tech stocks at one of the fastest paces on record last week as concerns that political opposition could derail the data-center buildout prompted a reassessment of the AI trade.

Citi strategists downgraded US stocks and global tech and upgraded European equities because of their lower exposure to AI, per Bloomberg. MarketWatch reported Citi said tech positioning needs to get cleaner before it would return to overweight.
Morgan Stanley's chief strategist said the correction is entering its final phase but advised waiting before buying the dip, per MarketWatch.
Asian equities mostly rebounded Monday after steep losses last week, per the Wall Street Journal; Bloomberg reported China's state-led funds bought a record amount of ETFs.

framing.note: Reuters headline puts Nvidia at the center of Monday's futures move and calls last week 'rough'.
Bloomberg's headline stresses hedge-fund selling pace and links it to political opposition to data centers.
MarketWatch frames it as a correction near its end, with advice to be patient before buying.

stories.headline: Strong October jobs report keeps a December Fed rate hike in play
stories.summary: October payrolls rose by 165,000, well above forecasts, and unemployment fell to 4.1%, according to reports found in search. Markets put about a 78% chance on a quarter-point Fed hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting, per Reuters as summarized by Kitco. Bloomberg reported gold held a decline as the jobs data fanned December hike bets.
stories.why_it_matters: A Fed that is still weighing rate increases keeps mortgage, car and credit-card borrowing costs high. A strong job market helps workers but can push rate cuts further away.
stories.background: The Fed raised its benchmark rate in September and held at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28, according to reports found in search. Kevin Warsh is the Fed chair and has kept open the option of more hikes while inflation is above the 2% target. Traders had trimmed hike bets amid the AI stock turmoil, and the jobs data reversed part of that. Next data points are October inflation in mid-November and the November jobs report on Dec. 4.

The WSJ reported US and eurozone government bond yields turned higher as investors refocused on economic data.

concept.explanation: A buyback is when a company uses its cash to purchase its own stock on the open market. That shrinks the number of shares outstanding, so each remaining share represents a larger slice of the company, which can lift earnings per share and often the stock price. Cash rich companies such as Berkshire Hathaway, which sped up buybacks this quarter, use them when they think the shares are cheap or have no better use for the money. It reaches your wallet through stock prices in retirement and brokerage accounts, but buybacks use money that could have gone to wages, research or dividends.
